new.title: Thermal emission spectroscopy of the ultra-hot Jupiter HAT-P-70b: NIRPS constraints on its refractory and volatile content
new.summary: Context. The chemical makeup of exoplanets provides insight into their origins and internal structures. High dayside temperatures on ultra-hot Jupiters vaporise refractory species and dissociate volatile molecules such as water. Cooler nightsides enable condensation (e.g. Fe) and cold-trapping (e.g. Ti), as compounds transition out of the gas phase. These contrasting conditions make dayside emission spectra a probe of both elemental inventories and atmospheric chemistry in the gas. Aim. We characterise the dayside atmosphere of the ultra-hot Jupiter HAT-P-70b via thermal emission spectroscopy, constraining its refractory and volatile budget and assessing thermal dissociation and cold-trapping. We focus on the abundances of rock-forming elements (Fe, Si, and Mg) and the depletion or survival of Ti and H2O. Methods. We analyse secondary-eclipse observations of HAT-P-70b acquired with NIRPS. From the emission spectrum, we infer the planet's atmospheric thermal structure and composition using a well-mixed retrieval framework. Results. We detect emission signatures from Fe, Mg, V, Si, and OH, but no significant H2O signal. The presence of OH and absence of water indicate strong thermal dissociation, with water likely depleted by more than 90% in the probed layers. The retrieved temperature profile shows a pronounced thermal inversion. Elemental abundance ratios (Fe/Si, Mg/Si, V/Si) are broadly consistent with solar-like composition, while titanium appears sub-solar, possibly due to partial condensation and nightside cold-trapping. Conclusions. HAT-P-70b's dayside atmosphere is dominated by refractory species and strong thermal processes. The detection of OH and absence of H2O indicate efficient water dissociation, while sub-solar titanium suggests nightside cold-trapping. Refractory element ratios are consistent with solar values, supporting a link between planetary and stellar compositions.
authors: Rillck Guilherme de Souza Barros de Amorim

new.title: The JWST Sub-Jupiters Survey: The impact of a large JWST/NIRCam PSF library on exoplanet imaging detection sensitivity
new.summary: The excellent infrared sensitivity of JWST allows direct imaging of young low-mass (below $\sim1$ M$_{\text{Jup}}$) giant planets for the first time, with several JWST programs being carried out for this purpose. However, the detection sensitivity of these observations crucially depends on subtracting the residual light of the host star to reveal faint astrophysical signals. This requires high quality observations of reference stars to build an empirical starlight model. Here we present a homogeneously processed reference star library of targets observed with programs GO 4050, GO 5835 and SURVEY 6005, which enable PSF subtraction via reference star differential imaging. These observations were taken with the MASK335R coronagraph mask and in dual-filter F444W/F200W mode. Our library consists of 247 observations (counting both filters separately) of 100 different stars of spectral types mostly F to M, with a total of 1110 individual integrations. We explore the PSF subtraction hyper-parameters with the KLIP algorithm (Soummer et al. 2012) that maximize sensitivity, and we show the performance of our library compared to and in addition to contemporaneous reference observations. We show that our library improves sensitivity at close separations in most tested cases, with improvement factors from $\sim1.3$ to $\sim2$ at some separations. As practical recommendations, we find that our library is best used as a complement to contemporaneous reference observations to further improve sensitivity, since in all our experiments contemporaneous references are needed for best sensitivity. We make the PSF library publicly available for the high-contrast imaging community.

new.title: Carbon dioxide and amorphous water ices in the debris disk around $β$ Pictoris
new.summary: The star $\beta$ Pictoris is orbited by a dusty debris disk, within which planet formation is occurring. The disk extends far from the star such that molecules in the outer disk should freeze. We observed the $\beta$ Pictoris disk in the near-infrared using the James Webb Space Telescope. The spectrum shows features due to amorphous water ice (<7% crystallinity), and carbon dioxide ice in both the $^{12}$CO$_2$ and $^{13}$CO$_2$ isotopologues. We infer that the CO$_2$ ice is intimately mixed with the water ice, at a ratio of 1:10. This implies that the ices formed in cold conditions, likely in the interstellar medium during a phase of amorphous H$_2$O-dominated formation. Frequent collisions within the debris disk are required to explain the observed uniform distribution of icy dust grains.

new.title: 3D Radiative Transfer Simulations for Characterization of the Optically Thick DART Ejecta Plume
new.summary: The Hyperion package is a three-dimensional Monte-Carlo radiative transfer approach to modeling dust ejecta. Because it has proven to be a powerful tool for simulating optically thick environments with complicated structure, we are applying the routines to observations of the DART impact on asteroid Dimorphos. Our analysis focuses on the LICIACube LUKE red-filter image acquired 175 s after impact, when the near-surface plume remained dense and not strongly structured. The model incorporates the updated Dimorphos shape model, spacecraft and solar geometry derived, and size-dependent scattering properties of realistic dust particles. We adopt an axisymmetric conical ejecta geometry and iteratively adjust the particle size distribution (PSD) and vertical number density profile to reproduce observed brightness profiles extracted from the LUKE image. We find that a power-law PSD with slope k = 3.0 and a number density peak located at approximately 120 m above the surface best reproduces the brightness contrast between the illuminated surface, the bright ejecta plume, and the adjacent dark band produced by shadowing within the optically thick material. The resulting best-fit model implies a total ejecta mass of 1.25 x 10^6 kg within 500 m of the impact site.

new.title: Comets in Kepler background photometry: the ion tail and tail disconnection of C/2009 K5 (McNaught) and an analysis of comets crossing the Kepler field
new.summary: Kepler recorded several thousand dedicated sky-background pixels per detector output every 29.4 min from 2009 to 2013, an archive that we use to study comets. During 2010 April 14-21 a narrow band of excess light swept across the field at 1.46 deg/day. This feature is the ion tail of comet C/2009 K5 (McNaught), whose head passed just beyond the edge of the detector array. We trace the tail from 0.9 deg to ~13 deg from the nucleus at surface brightnesses of 26.7-30 mag/arcsec^2; its aberration implies a solar-wind speed of ~500-750 km/s. At 30-min cadence we follow a tail-disconnection event on 2010 April 17-19 whose timing and geometry are consistent with a flank encounter with a coronal mass ejection, although other triggers cannot be excluded. We then analyze all 21 known comets with perihelion distance q < 15 AU whose heads crossed the detectors, using photometry at the predicted head positions calibrated against displaced control tracks. Eight comets are detected, including C/2010 J4 (WISE) a few days before its discovery and two comets at 6.3-7.4 AU with one-sided streaks that we interpret as dust tails. The undetected comets give 3-sigma limits of typically Kp > 16.6-18.1 within 5 arcmin of the head. A blind shift-and-stack search for moving diffuse sources, roughly 50% complete at Kp ~ 15.5-16 for rates of 0.3-1 deg/day, recovers four known comets and finds no unknown ones. Animations show the K5 tail and comets C/2011 L3 and C/2010 J4 crossing the field.

new.title: Detection of CH$_2$NH on Titan
new.summary: Saturn's moon, Titan, presents a chemical environment where abiotic synthesis of organics essential for life -- including amino acids and nucleotide bases -- may naturally occur. The assessment of Titan's organic content begins with characterizing its atmospheric chemical inventory, where many predicted molecular species remain unidentified. Here, we present the definitive spectroscopic detection of CH$_2$NH (methanimine) on Titan from observations with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array. CH$_2$NH represents the first stable imine (C=N) to be detected on Titan, and may be integral for further biomolecule formation as a precursor to glycine and adenine. We find abundances of CH$_2$NH at the 0.1--1 ppb level in Titan's mesosphere through multiple valid vertical profile configurations, yielding total column densities ranging from $\sim0.9$--$3\times10^{13}$ cm$^{-2}$. Middle-atmospheric abundances are commensurate with recent photochemical model predictions. However, models with parameterized galactic cosmic ray (GCR) fluxes, which exhibit a secondary, stratospheric formation site, are shown to provide poor fits to the data. Thus, our results provide confirmation of predicted formation and destruction pathways for CH$_2$NH in the upper atmosphere, and demonstrate secondary formation mechanisms in the lower atmosphere require adjustments. The latter presents an important barrier for fully estimating Titan's lower atmospheric composition, as enhanced production by GCR is predicted for additional N-bearing species, such as NH$_3$ and CH$_3$NH$_2$ (methylamine). The detection of CH$_2$NH provides the motivation to search for additional species fundamental for prebiotic molecule formation, which will dramatically improve our understanding of complex molecular synthesis of relevance to astrobiology in CH$_4$-rich environments.

new.title: OGLE-2018-BLG-0829L: A Microlensing System with a Planet Orbiting a Star Possessing a Brown-Dwarf Companion
new.summary: We analyze the microlensing event OGLE-2018-BLG-0829, whose light curve exhibits a weak short-term anomaly in addition to the prominent caustic-crossing features of a binary lens. The anomaly cannot be explained by a binary-lens single-source (2L1S) model. We therefore investigate both binary-lens binary-source (2L2S) and triple-lens single-source (3L1S) interpretations and find that both models reproduce the additional anomaly, with the 3L1S model being favored by $\Delta\chi^2=15.1$. Under the favored 3L1S interpretation, the anomaly arises from a caustic induced by a planetary-mass companion, whereas the prominent caustic-crossing features are produced by the underlying binary lens. Combining the measured event timescale, $t_{\rm E}=7.55\pm0.30$ days, and angular Einstein radius, $\theta_{\rm E}=0.325 \pm 0.059$ mas, with a Bayesian analysis, we infer a lens system consisting of an M dwarf of mass $0.193^{+0.300}_{-0.098}\,M_\odot$, a possible brown-dwarf companion of mass $0.068^{+0.105}_{-0.034}\,M_\odot$, and a Saturn-mass planet of mass $0.337^{+0.522}_{-0.171}\,M_{\rm J}$. The companions have projected separations of approximately 3.6 au and 1.6 au from the primary, respectively. However, the physical interpretation remains tentative because potentially important higher-order effects have not been considered, and the dynamical stability of the proposed configuration remains uncertain. If confirmed, this would be the third star--brown dwarf--planet system identified through microlensing, highlighting the potential of microlensing to detect planets in complex multiple systems.

new.title: High-inclination Centaur or Captured Halley-Type Comet? Observational and Dynamical Characterization of C/2024 L1 (PANSTARRS)
new.summary: The high-inclination (`high-i') Centaurs of the middle and outer Solar System are of uncertain origin. While many have been captured directly from the Oort Cloud, making them less-evolved analogues to the Halley-Type Comets, this process alone cannot produce the number of observed objects. The most discussed alternate origin is direct excitation of trans-Neptunian Objects into high-i orbits by the action of some unfound massive planet beyond Neptune. It is thus critical to find ways to discern the origins of these objects to provide new constraints on the various unfound planet hypotheses. This work assesses the only known active high-i Centaur: C/2024 L1 (PANSTARRS). Our dynamical investigations show that L1 has not decreased its semimajor axis in at least the past 1810 years, unlike all known TNO-derived active Centaurs at lower-i whose activity initiates after orbital changes. We also imaged L1 on five nights in the year before its April 2025 perihelion and found its brightness and optical colors to be stable and that its tail grew steadily. While this is like many Halley-type comets, few active low-i Centaurs have such stable activity. We thus propose that L1 is a captured Oort Cloud comet analogous to lower perihelion Halley-types and is thus a highly attractive target for large aperture follow up. The number and active fraction of these high-i objects should help us discern their origins and survey telescopes like Roman and Rubin could help us figure out where in the Outer Solar System the mystery lies.

new.title: A new chemical network to explore the disequilibrium chemistry of silicates and iron in hot gas giants
new.summary: Chemical equilibrium modeling of gas giant planet atmospheres has shown that the production and condensation of silicates plays an important role in shaping their final composition. However, no chemical kinetics network for these species are available, preventing the opportunity to analyze the impact of chemical disequilibrium processes. In this paper we present \texttt{SILANE}, a new chemical network that include Mg, Si, Fe and 15 carriers of these elements, including MgSiO$_3$ and Mg$_2$SiO$_4$, ready for use in the VULCAN code. We compare the results of our network with a chemical equilibrium model and discuss them in relation to previous results from literature. We then apply our new network to the analysis of a vertically mixed, Solar-composition atmosphere with equilibrium temperatures $T_{eq}$ in the [700, 1600] K range, finding that (i) rock-forming silicates disappears from the upper atmosphere already at 1100 K, (ii) SiH$_4$ reaches concentrations of $10^{-7}$ in the upper ($P\le 1.0$ bar) atmosphere for planets with $T_{eq}\in$ [800, 1100] K and (iii) the amount of oxygen in refractories decrease from 21\% at $T_{eq}$=700 K to essentially zero already at 1000 K, while in the classical equilibrium framework it remains constant up to $T_{eq}$=1300 K. By applying our network to the case of the young hot Jupiter YSES-1 c and comparing both the mixing ratios of volatile species and the enstatite fraction in the silicate mix, we find evidence of a well-mixed atmosphere, possibly with an average $K_{zz} \ge 10^{10}$ cm$^{2}$s$^{-1}$ up to the $10^{-4}$ bar level.

new.title: TOI-2665 b: A Highly Irradiated Giant in the Hot Neptune Desert
new.summary: We report the confirmation of TOI-2665 b, a close-in sub-Saturn ($P=2.85$ days, $R_p=7.00_{-0.15}^{+0.16}~R_{\oplus}$) just inside the hot Neptune desert around a metal-rich G dwarf, observed by the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS). We make use of the Carnegie Planet Finder Spectrograph for precise radial velocity measurements to measure its mass with $13.5\sigma$ precision ($M_p= 57.0_{-4.2}^{+4.2} ~M_{\oplus}$). The low density of TOI-2665 b ($\rho_{p} \sim 0.9~\mathrm{gcm}^{-3}$) implies the existence of a significant gaseous envelope that has survived in the hot Neptune desert despite high irradiation ($S=1068~S_{\oplus}$), making it an intriguing target for understanding the formation and evolution of desert-dwelling giants. The relatively bright host star ($V=11.0$ mag, $J=9.8$ mag) and extensive atmosphere make TOI-2665 b a promising target for atmospheric characterization.

new.title: Complex Interplay between Outer Disk Dynamics and Inner Water Reservoir
new.summary: We present a homogeneous characterization of outer disk dust and gas properties for 51 protoplanetary disks from the JWST/MIRI Cycle 1 programs, combining new ALMA observations with archival data. Visibility fitting with frank recovers more and higher-contrast substructures in the mm continuum than image-plane analysis, placing the innermost features of several disks at 4-5 au and leaving only three disks featureless at the current resolution. CO gas disk sizes span $\sim$60-1000 au and correlate strongly with mm continuum sizes, with $R_{\rm CO}/R_{\rm mm}$ ranging from 1.4 to 9.7 (median 2.95). We then connect these outer disk properties to JWST/MIRI inner disk water diagnostics. We find no global correlation between the cold-to-hot water flux ratio ($F_{\rm cold}/F_{\rm hot}$), a proposed proxy of cold water enrichment by pebble transport, and any single outer disk parameter, including $R_{\rm mm}$, $R_{\rm CO}/R_{\rm mm}$, and innermost substructure location. Three compact ($R_{\rm mm}<30$ au), structureless disks with $R_{\rm CO}/R_{\rm mm}>4$ show both elevated $F_{\rm cold}/F_{\rm hot}$ and cold water emission near the snowline temperature, consistent with unimpeded inward drift of icy pebbles. For structured disks, the water properties instead vary widely at fixed gap location, reflecting the sensitivity of the inner disk water content to multiple factors, including gap leakiness, grain size, and thermal history. Linking outer disk dust evolution to inner disk water content thus requires carefully selected samples with detailed constraints on these additional parameters.

new.title: Hemispheric asymmetry and up/down anisotropy of Jupiter's auroral electron precipitation: Juno/JEDI statistics
new.summary: Energetic electron precipitation shapes Jupiter's auroral emissions, thermal structure, and atmospheric chemistry. Whether its intensity differs between hemispheres, and whether that difference is consistent across auroral sub-regions, remains statistically unexplored over a large perijove sample. We statistically characterize the precipitating electron energy flux in Jupiter's auroral sub-regions, polar emission (PE) and main emission (ME), separating downward and upward fluxes and comparing hemispheres, using Juno/JEDI data from PJ3 to PJ66. Juno footprints from JRM33 and a current sheet model assign each spectrum to an auroral sub-region, where the downward and upward energy flux are integrated over the corresponding loss cone. The median energy flux differs between hemispheres by a factor of about two in the PE and the ME, for both flux directions, but the dominant hemisphere is reversed, the north dominating in the PE (N/S of 2.5 downward, 2.0 upward) and the south in the ME (0.65 and 0.5). The mean electron energy is nearly identical in both hemispheres in every sub-region, so the asymmetry lies in the number flux rather than the local acceleration efficiency. The PE also shows a systematic upward excess over downward flux in both hemispheres, maximal at the magnetic pole. The PE/ME reversal shows that the two hemispheres partition precipitated energy differently between the polar cap and the main oval. The PE anisotropy, qualitatively identical in both hemispheres, indicates that this partition is not driven by a hemispheric contrast in field-aligned acceleration efficiency.

new.title: Validation of Ariel candidates orbiting K-M stars
new.summary: One of the key goals of planetary population studies is to achieve broad coverage of the parameter space, which is not yet fully represented by confirmed planets. This limitation can be mitigated by including planets that have been statistically validated through a vetting procedure, even if they are not fully confirmed. In preparation for the Ariel mission, a Mission Candidate Sample has been assembled, comprising both confirmed planets and several unvalidated candidates. In this context, we apply a vetting analysis to a selected subsample of these candidates. Our methodology is based on the TRICERATOPS tool, aimed at confirming the presence of transiting planets or ruling out false-positive scenarios. We applied TRICERATOPS to a sample of 318 targets drawn from the last three Ariel TESS Planet Candidates catalogues. The analysis includes evaluation of statistical probabilities, as well as checks on stellar binarity indicators such as the Renormalized Unit Weight Error (RUWE) and the IPD_frac_multi_peak values from Gaia Data Release 3. Our analysis validated 56 candidates as planets, identified 29 false positives, and classified 35 as likely planets. These results are intended to support the Ariel mission by providing a probabilistic priority ranking to guide follow-up observations and optimise targets for atmospheric characterisation studies.

new.title: A First Look at Astrometric Outer Companions to Super-Earths and Sub-Neptunes using Gaia DR2 and DR3
new.summary: Massive outer companions (OCs) are believed to promote, inhibit, or otherwise regulate the formation and composition of inner small planets (ISPs) both in the solar system and in exoplanetary systems. To assess how, we leverage calibrated absolute astrometry from Gaia DR2-DR3 of 7,321 FGKM dwarfs and present measurements of the relative occurrence rate of OCs in systems hosting known ISPs (i.e. P(OC$|$ISP)/P(OC)), including systems with inner super-Earths only, inner sub-Neptunes only, and across a range of spectral types and stellar metallicities. We search for OCs in pairs of planet and reference stellar samples using the orbital fitting framework Octofitter and characterize the occurrence of OCs in mass--semi-major axis space under a Bayesian hierarchical model. We find an excess of OCs in systems with ISPs ($1.77\pm0.49$), independently supporting results from radial velocity surveys for the first time using astrometry. We recover similar excesses in both super-Earth (SE; $2.02\pm0.52$) and sub-Neptune systems (SN; $1.97\pm0.50$), highlighting that OCs do not inhibit the formation of ISPs, regardless of planet type. We argue that the consistency across SE and SN systems supports ex-situ formation, wherein ISPs form rapidly at larger separations prior to OCs opening disk gaps, thus providing evidence of Type I migration of SEs and SNs. We also evaluate how these results vary across stellar mass and metallicity, finding that M dwarfs exhibit an OC excess that is $1.41\pm0.78\times$ stronger than that around FGK dwarfs, and not finding a significant dependence on metallicity, contrary to previous radial velocity surveys.

new.title: The JWST Sub-Jupiters Survey: Observed Sensitivities to the Wide-Separation, Cold, Sub-Jupiter Exoplanet Population
new.summary: We present a sensitivity analysis of three recent JWST direct imaging programs (GO-4050, GO-5835, and SURVEY-6005) designed to build a demographic study of sub-Jupiter mass ($0.1 - 1$ M$_{\mathrm{J}}$) exoplanets in nearby young associations and moving groups. We find that these programs are sensitive to sub-Saturn to Jupiter mass exoplanets with effective temperature (T$_\mathrm{eff}$) as low as $\lesssim 250$ K, already at $\sim 2$ arcsec. A comparison with the SHINE survey confirms that the improvements in mass sensitivity provided by JWST high-contrast imaging surveys outpace current ground observation for masses $\lesssim 1$ M$_{\mathrm{J}}$ and separations between $\sim20-500$ au, opening up a novel parameter space to explore. Overall, this analysis provides a robust framework for interpreting future exoplanet detections. By correlating photometrically derived properties (e.g. mass, $T_{\mathrm{eff}}$, and separation) with theoretical model predictions, we show how the access to potentially low detectable masses (sub-Saturn to Jupiter) strongly depends on the expected atmospheric chemistry of the exoplanet population.

new.title: Compositions of Exoplanetary Debris Shaped by Milky Way Stellar Abundance Patterns
new.summary: Galactic chemical evolution (GCE) predicts large-scale variations in exoplanet compositions with host star elemental abundances, reflecting the Milky Way's history of star formation and elemental enrichment from stellar feedback. We investigate the impact of GCE on the compositions of exoplanetary bodies using polluted white dwarfs (WDs), which probe the bulk elemental abundances of planetary debris. Using a literature sample of 70 polluted WDs, we calculate iron mass fractions for the accreted bodies and compare these to tracers of the WD progenitor's initial abundances, including age and kinematics. We demonstrate predicted trends using a sample of main sequence stars, and we show that these are generally reflected in the polluted WD sample. In particular, H-dominated WDs show preferentially larger iron mass fractions amongst younger and less dynamically excited systems. This trend is weaker amongst He-dominated WDs, and we show that this may be attributed to uncertainties in their observed phases of accretion. Continuing to combine WD pollution compositions with stellar parameters and kinematics could be a valuable way to constrain large-scale versus local drivers of planetary compositions.

cross.title: Kepler as an accidental heliospheric imager: Thomson-scattered solar-wind structure in four years of background photometry
cross.summary: Kepler recorded several thousand dedicated sky-background pixels per detector output every 29.4 min from 2009 May to 2013 May while staring at a fixed 12-degree field at ecliptic latitude +65 degrees. From this archive we isolate a large-scale layer that measures brightness variations relative to an 8-day running median. This layer contains fluctuations of 0.02-0.1 electrons per second per pixel (about 1e-17 of the mean solar surface brightness) that sweep across the field in a day or less. Four lines of evidence show that these are sunlight Thomson-scattered by solar-wind electrons. (1) The sweeps propagate away from the Sun (84 percent within 45 degrees of the anti-solar direction; 25 percent expected by chance), and their direction follows the Sun through each quarter and across all 16 spacecraft rolls. (2) The field brightness correlates with the near-Earth (OMNI) proton density within a day of zero lag (r = 0.19, p < 1/150), but not with the energetic-proton flux. (3) Time-elongation maps show fronts moving outward at a median 15 degrees per day, as forward models of radially moving density structures predict. (4) The amplitude is about one third of a parameter-free Thomson-scattering prediction and varies by a factor of about 3 over the year, as predicted. Half of the scattered light comes from within 0.4-0.7 AU of the spacecraft. Fronts are strongest in slow wind. Kepler's background pixels thus provide a four-year, high-cadence, out-of-ecliptic record of solar-wind structure near 1 AU. Standard Kepler processing removes these signals, changing stellar light curves by less than about 1 ppm.

cross.title: Geometric tracking of a halo CME using full-circle wide-field views from PUNCH
cross.summary: We tracked the large, geoeffective halo coronal mass ejection (CME) of 2025-May-31 across the very wide field of view of the Polarimeter to Unify the Corona and Heliosphere (PUNCH) mission, as a proof of concept for data-informed forecasting of CME arrival times at Earth. using simple point-and-click measurement of the front location as far as 47 degrees away from the Sun itself, we constrained an analytic "ludicrous ice-cream cone" geometric model with just three parameters: position angle, off-Earth-Sun angle, and propagation speed. We show that the model is sufficient to capture the bulk envelope of the CME, and also insufficient to capture the complexity of the CME's evolution. We generated simulated arrival-time forecasts for the CME by extrapolating the constant-velocity propagation to determine the time of impact with Earth. These "retro-forecasts" converged to within 30 +/- 15 minutes of the actual arrival time, 8 hours prior to arrival. The convergence was marked by a clear inflection point in the curve of predicted-arrival-time vs time-of-forecast. We conclude that continuous wide-field tracking is sufficiently powerful to enable even crude models to substantially improve arrival-time forecasting precision, and discuss future work required both to validate this single-event result and to extend it to more sophisticated analyses.

cross.title: Magnetic Power in Binaries: From Coalescing Binary Neutron Stars to Close-in Exoplanetary Systems
cross.summary: A binary system containing two magnetic components ("stars") can be modeled as a circuit powered by the orbital motion, with the magnetic field lines linking the two stars serving as wires. When the total resistance in the binary components is small -- as found in many astrophysical systems such as binary neutron stars and extra-solar hot-Jupiter or super-Earth systems -- the connected field lines are twisted and open up in a quasi-cyclic manner, leading to quasi-periodic energy dissipation and flares. We derive analytic expressions for the average and episodic magnetic powers from such systems, providing a quantitative description on how the powers depend on the magnetic orientations of the two stars. The power can be much larger than in the case where one of the stars has a negligible magnetic field. It may manifest as pre-merger quasi-cyclic flares in coalescing neutron-star binaries and as orbit-regulated radio emissions in exoplanetary systems.

cross.title: XRISM/Xtend detection of solar wind charge exchange induced by multiple coronal mass ejections in 2024 August
cross.summary: Solar wind charge exchange (SWCX) emission is often a major component of the soft X-ray background, but it also provides a remote diagnostic of the composition and ionization state of solar wind plasma. We present an analysis of a SWCX event observed with XRISM/Xtend during 2024 August 9-13. The event occurred during intense solar activity with multiple flares, including an X1.3-class solar flare, and associated coronal mass ejections (CMEs). We found a clear enhancement in the 0.3-3.0 keV count rate that occurred nearly simultaneously with an increase in the solar wind proton flux measured by ACE. We fitted the spectrum during the enhancement period with a set of Gaussian emission lines. In addition to the commonly detected C, N, and O lines, we detected Ne, Mg, Si, and Fe lines at $>15\sigma$ significance. We extracted two characteristic periods within the enhanced interval based on the CME arrival timeline. The O$_{\rm VIII}$/Si$_{\rm XIII}$ line ratio changed significantly between the two periods, suggesting contributions from multiple CME components. We then applied the AtomDB charge exchange model with a multi-temperature setup. The estimated ionization temperatures for Ne, Mg, Si, and Fe increased with the peak soft X-ray flux of the associated solar flares. This trend suggests that coronal heating becomes more efficient for more intense flares. Meanwhile, the ionization temperatures were lower than typical flare electron temperatures, implying that CME plasma may have been released into interplanetary space under non-equilibrium ionization conditions. We also found an indication of an inverse-FIP pattern, with reduced relative abundances of Si and S. These results demonstrate that XRISM/Xtend can diagnose the coronal plasma through SWCX emission, including heavy ions such as Ne, Mg, and Si, which are difficult to measure with current in-situ instruments (e.g., ACE satellite).

cross.title: Simulating high-speed solar wind streams from coronal holes using an L5-L1 configuration of Lagrangian points
cross.summary: Coronal holes (CHs) are known to be sources of high-speed solar wind streams (HSSs), yet the physical mechanisms linking CH position and characteristics to solar wind (SW) behaviour remain unclear. Our results reveal that the latitude of CHs, especially smaller ones, combined with the heliographic latitude of the solar disk's central point (B0 angle), plays a critical role in driving discrepancies in SW velocity across the heliosphere. To investigate this, we use archival data from STEREO-B, STEREO-A, and Earth to simulate an L5-L1 configuration, where L5 is a vantage point approximately behind Earth in its orbit (as proposed for the Vigil mission), and L1 is between Earth and the Sun where SW measurements are typically taken. We use these insights to develop a predictive algorithm for HSSs, beginning with an analysis of the separation angle and distances between L5 and L1. We then introduce a predictive indicator and empirical criteria based on CH properties and the B0 angle to adjust for changes in SW velocity at L1. Our results show that the L5 viewpoint demonstrates the capability to significantly improve the accuracy and lead times of HSS predictions, enhancing our understanding of the CH-HSS relationship and potentially improving space weather forecasting.

cross.title: Observing Earth's ionospheric irregularities from the Moon
cross.summary: Radio signals that propagate through the Earth's ionosphere carry information about possible irregular plasma structures. Such irregularities manifest themselves as amplitude signatures that depend on the propagation and observation geometry [1, 2]. Conventional ground and low-Earth-orbit (LEO) measurements sample these effects close to Earth. Here we present a systematic characterization of terrestrial ionospheric irregularities using Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) amplitude observations from the lunar surface, at distances of approximately 356,000-398,000 km from Earth's surface [3]. Using nearly 93 h of 1-Hz lunar-surface observations of GPS L1/L5 and Galileo E1/E5a collected by the Lunar GNSS Receiver Experiment (LuGRE), we reconstruct the propagation and scanning geometry to characterize the spatiotemporal signatures of amplitude and phase fluctuations. At lunar distance, the Fresnel scale approaches its finite-source limit, extending the observations to a propagation regime beyond conventional near-Earth configurations. Detrended receiver-reported carrier-to-noise density ratios (${\delta}C/N_0$) reveal pronounced polar amplitude fluctuations at both frequency bands, also visible in the original measurements. Within the regions and local times sampled, large fluctuations occur in about 30% of valid one-minute polar windows, compared with less than 5% in either the equatorial or mid-latitude band. These findings support using the lunar surface as a vantage point for studying Earth's polar ionospheric irregularities and testing how propagation and scanning relative to the magnetic field shape their amplitude signatures. Future lunar observations could extend this approach to long-term monitoring of Earth's ionospheric irregularities

cross.title: Why Cassini's Oval Could Not Replace Kepler's Ellipse?
cross.summary: In the later seventeenth century, Kepler's ellipse was not yet accepted. Ward claimed that Boulliau's conic hypothesis amounted to a Ptolemaic equant at the ellipse's empty focus, and built his own model on it. Around 1675--1680, Giovanni Domenico Cassini proposed another curve, the ``oval'', a genus-1 quartic with no closed-form Kepler equation; yet its eccentric anomaly shares exactly the leading coefficient of Kepler's, and its empty focus is, for the Sun, 38 times closer to a true equant than the ellipse's. Dynamically, Binet's formula shows that the force producing the oval under the area law departs from the inverse square by an index $\mathcal{D}(e)\sim3/(4e^2)$, depending on the oval's parameter $e$: no single exponent serves the whole family. This absence of universality, not of an area law, distinguishes it from the ellipse, and arguably explains why Cassini, the Académie and Leibniz kept the question open after the \emph{Principia} (1687).

cross.title: Scaling of impact ripples across planetary conditions
cross.summary: Ubiquitous wind-driven (aeolian) ripples have been thought to emerge solely from grain collisions with the bed during saltation. Recent findings, however, have shown that there are two scales of aeolian ripples, with the larger scale having a hydrodynamic origin, akin to water ripples, and the smaller scale ('impact ripples') being hypothesized to emerge from the grain-bed collision mechanism. Still, there are several instances where only one ripple scale is found and the formation mechanism is not clear. Here we compare numerical simulations of only impact ripples with observations, over a broad range of planetary conditions, to clarify their defining characteristics. We find two main regimes for the scaling of impact ripple wavelengths based on transport intensity: for low-intensity transport ('saltation' regime), impact ripple wavelengths scale with grain size regardless of the fluid density; whereas for high-intensity transport ('collisional' regime) wavelengths scale with the average hoplength and thus increase with the fluid velocity. In contrast, impact ripple migration speeds strongly depend on the grain-fluid density ratio, grain size and fluid velocity. Finally, we find that impact ripple speeds become zero or negative (denoting stationary ripples and antiripples, respectively) for grain-fluid density ratios below a threshold that depends on the grain size. In particular, for low density ratios, like those found on Venus, or millimeter-scale grains on Earth, we find only antiripples. Our results thus provide a general framework for interpreting ripple emergence across environments and for identifying impact ripples in ambiguous field or experimental data.

repl.title: Micron-Scale Technosignatures: How a Cubic Metre of Lunar Regolith May Begin to Constrain the Number of Past Technological Civilisations in the Galaxy
repl.summary: Building on Arkhipov's proposal that technogenic artefacts may survive natural interstellar transport and accumulate on Solar System surfaces, we examine the prospects for identifying micron-scale engineered particulate material within the lunar regolith. We analyse the transport of micron and submicron grains through the interstellar medium, including gas drag, sputtering, and ISM phase-dependent survival, and show that refractory particles with characteristic radii of order 0.3 microns may traverse kiloparsec scales over residence times of 0.1-1 Gyr. Solar radiation pressure and heliospheric filtering define a dynamically constrained slow-arrival channel in which a small fraction of grains reach the Earth-Moon system at relative velocities compatible with survival upon impact. Combining these properties with regolith-mixing constraints yields quantitative upper limits on the cumulative undirected technomaterial output of large-scale spacefaring civilisations: a null detection in a cubic metre of regolith excludes scenarios in which Solar-type stars typically disperse more than approximately 0.10 Earth mass equivalents of long-lived artificial particulate debris over Galactic history. Deliberate targeting of the inner Solar System with artificial particulate matter defines a complementary regime characterised by the visitation frequency and deposited mass of such releases, for which the probabilities of detection may be orders of magnitude higher. We outline a multi-modal detection strategy integrating machine-vision triage with laboratory forensic techniques to identify anomalous grains within a well-characterised natural background. Particulate technosignatures thus establish an experimentally accessible form of exo-archaeology, capable of placing meaningful constraints -- and, in favourable cases, yielding direct material evidence -- of the Galaxy's technological history.

repl.title: Activity in White Dwarf Debris Disks II: WISE Mission Traces a Decade of Disk Evolution and Persistence
repl.summary: This study presents multi-epoch photometry from the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer to investigate variability in white dwarf debris disks, utilizing the full 14.5 yr mission datasets pre- and post-cryogen. Unambiguous variations are detected across the bulk of the 52 confirmed dusty white dwarfs and are consistent with universal variability after correcting for the sensitivity of WISE relative to Spitzer. Some disk light curves exhibit trends such as possible oscillations, sudden brightening, and steadily decaying fluxes, but all infrared excesses persist utterly. On baselines longer than 0.5 yr, flux changes are significantly skewed toward decreases, in contrast to the symmetric distribution found at shorter baselines with Spitzer, consistent with gradual dust depletion over time. Disk emission generally becomes redder when dimmer and bluer when brighter, consistent with changes in the grain size distribution following collisions, although five disks exhibit the opposite trend possibly due to dust production near apastron. A moderate positive correlation is observed between disk luminosity and photospheric Ca abundance, consistent with the accretion of disk material in an optically thin configuration. Taken together with the Spitzer legacy of dusty white dwarfs, these results provide a comprehensive view of debris disk variability and provide empirical constraints on models of disk structure and evolution.

repl.title: DART ejecta reveal the recoil momentum budget of a kinetic impact
repl.summary: Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) demonstrated that ejecta recoil enhances asteroid deflection, but the ejecta processes generating and distributing this recoil remained unclear. We reconstruct three-dimensional ejecta evolution from time-resolved morphology and brightness observations, recovering previously missing constraints on momentum transfer and material transport. Integrating reconstructed momentum yields momentum enhancement factors $\beta_\mathrm{D}=2.13 \pm 0.19 (1{\sigma})$ for Dimorphos and $\beta_\mathrm{sys}=2.04 \pm 0.19 (1{\sigma})$ for the Didymos system. Combined with the measured deflection, the reconstructed recoil constrains Dimorphos's bulk density to $1435.18_{-153.71}^{+112.59} \mathrm{kg m^{-3}}$ without assuming its mass. By linking observed orbital deflection to the released material, this reconstruction provides ejecta-based constraints for assessing kinetic-impact effectiveness and investigating how natural collisions drive mass loss and debris transport among small Solar System bodies.

repl.title: KRONOS II: Solar-like Umbra and Penumbra Properties on the Young Sun V1298~Tau
repl.summary: Transiting exoplanets provide a unique laboratory for studying stellar surface heterogeneities via starspot or facular occultations. When observed at multiple wavelengths, this configuration enables spectroscopic characterization of spot thermal contrasts, distributions, and morphology. In this work, we leverage JWST NIRISS/SOSS transit observations of the 20--30 Myr planets V1298~Tau~bcd to study the surface properties of their solar analog host star V1298~Tau. We identify 14 starspot crossing events across two visits. We derive $0.8-2.8\mu$m starspot contrast spectra and demonstrate the contrasts are best explained when accounting for the umbral and penumbral components of the starspots, robust to which stellar model grid is assumed. The spot temperatures are broadly consistent between visits, suggesting that V1298 Tau ($T_\mathrm{phot}=4866\pm33$ K) has starspots with $T_{\mathrm{umbra}}$ = 3200--3400 K umbrae and $T_{\mathrm{penumbra}}$ = 4400--4600 K penumbrae, and are $\sim$25--30\% umbrae by area. The differences between these spot components and the stellar photosphere are consistent with sunspots. Additionally, the relation between the spot contrast and the ratio of umbral to penumbral area is similar to that of the Sun. Combining these JWST observations with long baseline multi-band photometry from the Las Cumbres Observatory, we also estimated the global unocculted spot distribution, revealing at least 5 additional large unocculted active regions assuming no facular contribution. Altogether, these measurements suggest that while the total spot coverage evolves in time, the relative temperatures of surface heterogeneities on Sun-like stars may be consistent throughout their lifetimes. Furthermore, these results demonstrate that JWST exoplanet transit observations can be useful for starspot substructure characterization.
